title: Supplementary analyses: Human disturbance and the magnitude of phenotypic divergence
text:
0.1 About this supplement
This computational supplement accompanies the manuscript:
It documents every analytical step, from data import to final figures, in a reproducible Quarto book. All code is written in R and all models are fitted with brms using the cmdstanr backend.

title: Supplementary analyses: Human disturbance and the magnitude of phenotypic divergence
text: Human disturbance and the magnitude of phenotypic divergence: a Bayesian meta-regression of lnM across the PROCEED database.

title: Supplementary analyses: Human disturbance and the magnitude of phenotypic divergence
text:
0.2 The PROCEED database
The analyses use the PROCEED v6.2 database of rates of evolutionary and phenotypic change. Each row represents one contrast between two populations or time points, with the raw summary statistics (means, standard deviations, sample sizes) needed to compute an effect size.

title: Supplementary analyses: Human disturbance and the magnitude of phenotypic divergence
text:
0.3 The effect size: lnM
The central effect size is \(\ln M\) — the log ratio of the geometric mean absolute deviation from the trait mean. For independent-groups contrasts, \(\ln M\) is estimated using the SAFE (Simulation-based Adjusted For Estimation error) procedure implemented in orchaRd:::.safe_lnM_indep(). The SAFE estimator uses Monte Carlo sampling to propagate uncertainty from small samples and avoids the bias of naive estimators when sample sizes are small.
A positive \(\ln M\) indicates that the later or disturbed population shows greater phenotypic dispersion than the reference population. A value of zero indicates equal dispersion.

title: Supplementary analyses: Human disturbance and the magnitude of phenotypic divergence
text:
0.4 Location–scale meta-regression
The central statistical framework is location–scale meta-regression implemented in brms. Each model has the conceptual form:
bf(
  yi_lnM_safe ~ moderator + random_effects,
  sigma ~ moderator
)
The location submodel asks whether a moderator predicts the average magnitude of phenotypic divergence (\(\overline{\ln M}\)). The scale submodel asks whether the same moderator predicts the residual variation — the degree to which divergence is consistent (low \(\sigma\)) or heterogeneous (high \(\sigma\)) after accounting for the location effect.
One independent model per moderator. No large multi-moderator model is fitted. This ensures that each moderator’s effect is estimated from all data available for that moderator, and that no moderator’s influence is masked by collinearity with others.

title: Supplementary analyses: Human disturbance and the magnitude of phenotypic divergence
text:
0.5 Random effects
Every main model includes:

(1 | ref_id) — non-independence among contrasts from the same reference.
(1 | gr(sp_ncbi, cov = A)) — phylogenetic relatedness among species.
(1 | gr(es_id_model, cov = V)) — known sampling variance (SAFE estimates), using the brms known-variance trick with a constant(1) prior on the corresponding SD.

sys_id (study system) is reserved for sensitivity analyses because it is highly associated with ref_id and sp_ncbi and can make variance components hard to identify.

title: 3  lnM effect sizes (SAFE)
text:
3.1 What lnM measures
This chapter computes the effect size used throughout the book: \(\ln M\), the log magnitude of separation between two groups. The key idea is to measure how far apart two group means are without retaining the sign of the difference. This is useful here because human disturbance can push traits in different directions across systems, but the biological question is often about the magnitude of phenotypic divergence.
For a two-group comparison, \(\ln M\) is defined as:
\[
\ln M = \ln\left(\frac{s_B}{s_W}\right),
\]
where \(s_B\) is the between-group separation component and \(s_W\) is the pooled within-group standard deviation. The sign of \(\ln M\) is therefore not the direction of trait change. Instead:
This differs from taking an absolute value of a signed effect size such as \(|d|\) or \(|\ln RR|\). Absolute-value transformations fold sampling error around zero, which can inflate small and noisy effects. The lnM paper develops \(\ln M\) so that magnitude can be analysed directly with standard meta-analytic and meta-regression tools.

title: 3  lnM effect sizes (SAFE)
text:
\(\ln M > 0\) means the separation between group means is larger than the typical within-group standard deviation.
\(\ln M = 0\) means the between-group separation is about equal to the within-group standard deviation.
\(\ln M < 0\) means the groups differ, if at all, by less than the typical within-group variation.

title: 3  lnM effect sizes (SAFE)
text:
3.2 Why SAFE is used here
Analytic \(\ln M\) is built from ANOVA mean-square components. That construction is intuitive, but it has two practical problems for large ecological databases:

Sampling variance can become very large when the between-group mean square is close to the within-group mean square.
The plug-in estimate is undefined when the observed between-group component is not positive.

The SAFE estimator used below follows the paper’s simulation-based approach. For each contrast, it repeatedly draws plausible values of the group means and standard deviations from their finite-sample distributions, transforms each valid draw to \(\ln M\), and then summarizes the resulting distribution. This gives a finite bias-adjusted estimate and sampling variance for contrasts that would otherwise be unstable or undefined.
The book uses the cached SAFE results by default. Recomputing all contrasts is intentionally opt-in because the Monte Carlo step is slow.

SAFE only summarizes valid simulation draws, so the retained-draw diagnostics are important. A low retained percentage means many simulated draws landed in the region where the between-group component was non-positive; those contrasts are still usable, but their uncertainty should be interpreted with care.

    n_ok           = sum(status == "ok"),
    n_not_ok       = sum(status != "ok"),
    min_pct_kept   = round(min(draws_kept / draws_total * 100), 1),
    median_pct_kept = round(median(draws_kept / draws_total * 100), 1),

title: 5  Dependency structure
text:
5.2 Why dependency matters
Multiple contrasts in a meta-analysis often share a reference (same paper), a study system (same population or location), or a species. Ignoring this non-independence inflates effective sample size and narrows credible intervals inappropriately. Random effects in the location–scale model account for three sources of dependency:

Reference (ref_id) — contrasts from the same paper share design choices, sampling effort, and measurement protocol.
Phylogenetic relatedness (sp_ncbi, via A) — species that share evolutionary history have correlated trait values.
Sampling variance (es_id_model, via V) — each contrast has a known estimation error (from SAFE) that is treated as a fixed component rather than estimated.

sys_id (study system) is correlated with both ref_id and sp_ncbi in these data, which makes it hard to identify a separate system-level variance component. It is therefore reserved for sensitivity analyses.

5.3 Nesting diagnostic helper


Code
check_nesting <- function(data, a, b) {
  tmp <- data |>
    dplyr::count(.data[[a]], .data[[b]], name = "n") |>
    dplyr::count(.data[[a]], name = "n_unique_b")

  tibble::tibble(
    factor_a              = a,
    factor_b              = b,
    n_levels_a            = dplyr::n_distinct(data[[a]]),
    n_levels_b            = dplyr::n_distinct(data[[b]]),
    min_unique_b_per_a    = min(tmp$n_unique_b),
    median_unique_b_per_a = stats::median(tmp$n_unique_b),
    max_unique_b_per_a    = max(tmp$n_unique_b),
    prop_a_single_b       = mean(tmp$n_unique_b == 1),
    a_nested_in_b         = all(tmp$n_unique_b == 1)
  )
}

section: 5.9 Species coverage for phylogenetic random effect
text:
5.9 Species coverage for phylogenetic random effect
Before fitting any model it is useful to know how many rows will be affected by the phylogenetic alignment step. Two sources of row loss are distinguished:

sp_ncbi is NA or blank — the contrast has no species information at all. These rows are always excluded from any species-level random effect.
Valid sp_ncbi not matched in the Open Tree of Life — the species name exists in the data but rotl could not retrieve it during tree construction. Under the default fill_unmatched = TRUE behaviour these species are retained in the model and assigned zero phylogenetic correlation with all other species (a “star” contribution). They are not silently dropped.



Code
source(here::here("R", "05_phylogeny.R"))

A_full   <- tryCatch(readRDS(here::here("outputs", "phylogeny", "proceed_A_matrix.rds")),
                     error = function(e) NULL)
name_map <- tryCatch(readRDS(here::here("outputs", "phylogeny", "proceed_name_map.rds")),
                     error = function(e) NULL)

if (!is.null(A_full) && !is.null(name_map)) {
  dat_coverage <- apply_phylo_name_map(dat_es, name_map)

  sp_raw       <- as.character(dat_es$sp_ncbi)
  sp_canonical <- as.character(dat_coverage$sp_ncbi_canonical)

  n_na_raw       <- sum(is.na(sp_raw) | sp_raw == "")
  n_named        <- sum(!is.na(sp_raw) & nzchar(sp_raw))
  n_resolved     <- sum(!is.na(sp_canonical) & nzchar(sp_canonical))
  n_unresolved   <- n_named - n_resolved

  sp_uniq_can    <- unique(sp_canonical[!is.na(sp_canonical) & nzchar(sp_canonical)])
  sp_in_tree     <- sp_uniq_can[sp_uniq_can %in% rownames(A_full)]
  sp_star        <- setdiff(sp_uniq_can, rownames(A_full))

  tibble::tibble(
    Category = c(
      "Total contrasts",
      "sp_ncbi is NA / blank (no species info)",
      "Named species — resolved to canonical name",
      "Named species — unresolved after 4-stage cascade",
      "Unique canonical species in phylogenetic tree",
      "Unique canonical species assigned star (zero) correlation"
    ),
    N = c(
      nrow(dat_es),
      n_na_raw,
      n_resolved,
      n_unresolved,
      length(sp_in_tree),
      length(sp_star)
    )
  )
} else {
  cat("Phylogeny / name map not yet built. Run chapter 05 first.\n")
}

title: 5  Dependency structure
text:
5.10 Random-effects rationale
The nesting diagnostics above reveal:

es_id_db is the finest-grained identifier (one row per contrast) and is nested within all higher-level groupings.
Most studies (ref_id) contribute data from one system, but a meaningful fraction contribute from multiple systems.
Most species (sp_ncbi) appear in one system, but some span multiple systems and references.
Systems can span multiple references and species, creating a crossed (not purely hierarchical) structure.

This crossed structure means that ref_id and sp_ncbi (via phylogeny) can both be estimated in the same model. Adding sys_id as a third group-level predictor in this crossed design risks near-collinearity with ref_id and sp_ncbi, making variance components weakly identified. For this reason, sys_id is included in sensitivity analyses only.

title: 6  Location–scale model grid
text:
6.4 Fit or read models
The loop below iterates over every row of the registry. For each moderator it:

Checks the moderator exists and has enough data.
Drops rows missing that moderator.
Rebuilds the sequential es_id_model and sampling-variance matrix V.
Subsets the phylogenetic matrix A to the species present.
Builds the formula and priors.
Calls fit_or_read_model(), which reads the cached .rds if it exists.
Extracts summaries and diagnostics.



Code
# Heavy path (rebuild_grid = TRUE only): load every model and extract summaries.
# Normal renders skip this and read the precomputed cache below.
all_fe    <- list()
all_diag  <- list()
status_rows <- list()

for (i in seq_len(nrow(moderator_grid))) {
  row        <- moderator_grid[i, ]
  mod_id     <- row$model_id
  moderator  <- row$moderator
  mod_label  <- row$label
  mod_type   <- row$type
  model_file <- paste0(mod_id, "_ls_", moderator)

  message("\n--- ", mod_id, ": ", moderator, " ---")

  # ── 1. Check moderator exists ──────────────────────────────────────────────
  if (!moderator %in% names(dat_es)) {
    status_rows[[i]] <- tibble::tibble(
      model_id = mod_id, moderator = moderator, label = mod_label,
      type = mod_type, n_rows = 0L, n_levels = NA_integer_,
      n_missing_excluded = NA_integer_,
      model_path = NA_character_, status = "skipped: variable absent",
      notes = "Moderator not found in dataset.",
      max_rhat = NA_real_, min_bulk_ess = NA_real_, min_tail_ess = NA_real_,
      n_divergent = NA_integer_, max_treedepth_hits = NA_integer_
    )
    next
  }

  # ── 2. Subset data for this moderator ─────────────────────────────────────
  n_before     <- nrow(dat_es)
  dat_model    <- dat_es[!is.na(dat_es[[moderator]]), ]
  n_missing_ex <- n_before - nrow(dat_model)

  if (mod_type == "categorical") {
    dat_model[[moderator]] <- droplevels(factor(dat_model[[moderator]]))
  }

  # Check sample size per level for categorical moderators
  n_levels <- NA_integer_
  level_counts <- NULL
  if (mod_type == "categorical") {
    level_counts <- table(dat_model[[moderator]])
    n_levels     <- length(level_counts)
    sparse       <- level_counts[level_counts < 5]
    if (length(sparse) > 0) {
      message("Sparse levels (<5 obs) in ", moderator, ": ",
              paste(names(sparse), collapse = ", "))
    }
    if (all(level_counts < 3)) {
      status_rows[[i]] <- tibble::tibble(
        model_id = mod_id, moderator = moderator, label = mod_label,
        type = mod_type, n_rows = nrow(dat_model), n_levels = n_levels,
        n_missing_excluded = n_missing_ex,
        model_path = NA_character_, status = "skipped: too sparse",
        notes = "All levels have fewer than 3 observations.",
        max_rhat = NA_real_, min_bulk_ess = NA_real_, min_tail_ess = NA_real_,
        n_divergent = NA_integer_, max_treedepth_hits = NA_integer_
      )
      next
    }
  }

  if (nrow(dat_model) < 10) {
    status_rows[[i]] <- tibble::tibble(
      model_id = mod_id, moderator = moderator, label = mod_label,
      type = mod_type, n_rows = nrow(dat_model), n_levels = n_levels,
      n_missing_excluded = n_missing_ex,
      model_path = NA_character_, status = "skipped: insufficient data",
      notes = paste("Only", nrow(dat_model), "rows after missingness exclusion."),
      max_rhat = NA_real_, min_bulk_ess = NA_real_, min_tail_ess = NA_real_,
      n_divergent = NA_integer_, max_treedepth_hits = NA_integer_
    )
    next
  }

  # ── 3 & 4. Align data to phylogeny, build V ─────────────────────────────────
  # prepare_phylo_and_data() subsets A to species present in this model's data,
  # filters dat_model to the intersection (so every sp_ncbi level is in A),
  # rebuilds es_id_model sequentially, and constructs the diagonal V matrix.
  dat_model <- dat_model |>
    dplyr::mutate(es_id_model = factor(seq_len(dplyr::n())))

  phylo     <- prepare_phylo_and_data(dat_model, A_full, label = mod_id)
  dat_model <- phylo$dat_model
  A_mod     <- phylo$A_mod
  V         <- phylo$V
  has_phylo <- phylo$has_phylo

  # ── 5. Build formula and priors ───────────────────────────────────────────
  formula <- build_ls_formula(moderator, has_phylogeny = has_phylo)
  priors  <- build_ls_priors(formula, dat_model, V, A = A_mod)

  # ── 5b. Verify constant(1) is correctly set before any fitting ────────────
  prior_ok <- verify_esid_prior(priors, model_name = mod_id)
  if (!prior_ok) {
    status_rows[[i]] <- tibble::tibble(
      model_id = mod_id, moderator = moderator, label = mod_label,
      type = mod_type, n_rows = nrow(dat_model), n_levels = n_levels,
      n_missing_excluded = n_missing_ex,
      model_path = NA_character_, status = "skipped: prior check failed",
      notes = "constant(1) was not confirmed at coef=Intercept level for es_id_model.",
      max_rhat = NA_real_, min_bulk_ess = NA_real_, min_tail_ess = NA_real_,
      n_divergent = NA_integer_, max_treedepth_hits = NA_integer_
    )
    next
  }

  # ── 6. Fit or read ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  model_path_full <- file.path(
    here::here("outputs", "models"),
    paste0(model_file, ".rds")
  )

  fit <- tryCatch({
    fit_or_read_model(
      model_name = model_file,
      fit_fun    = function() {
        fit_ls_model(dat_model, formula, priors,
                     V = V, A = A_mod,
                     mcmc_args = default_mcmc_args)
      },
      model_dir  = here::here("outputs", "models"),
      refit      = refit_models
    )
  }, error = function(e) {
    message("Model fitting failed for ", moderator, ": ", conditionMessage(e))
    NULL
  })

  # ── 7. Extract summaries and diagnostics ──────────────────────────────────
  if (is.null(fit)) {
    status_rows[[i]] <- tibble::tibble(
      model_id = mod_id, moderator = moderator, label = mod_label,
      type = mod_type, n_rows = nrow(dat_model), n_levels = n_levels,
      n_missing_excluded = n_missing_ex,
      model_path = model_path_full, status = "failed",
      notes = "Model returned NULL (fitting error).",
      max_rhat = NA_real_, min_bulk_ess = NA_real_, min_tail_ess = NA_real_,
      n_divergent = NA_integer_, max_treedepth_hits = NA_integer_
    )
    next
  }

  fe   <- extract_fixed_effects(fit, mod_id, moderator)
  diag <- tryCatch(
    extract_diagnostics(fit, mod_id, moderator),
    error = function(e) {
      message("Diagnostics failed for ", moderator, ": ", conditionMessage(e))
      tibble::tibble(
        model_id = mod_id, moderator = moderator,
        max_rhat = NA_real_, min_bulk_ess = NA_real_,
        min_tail_ess = NA_real_, n_divergent = NA_integer_,
        max_treedepth_hits = NA_integer_
      )
    }
  )

  all_fe[[mod_id]]   <- split_location_scale(fe)
  all_diag[[mod_id]] <- diag

  status_rows[[i]] <- tibble::tibble(
    model_id           = mod_id,
    moderator          = moderator,
    label              = mod_label,
    type               = mod_type,
    n_rows             = nrow(dat_model),
    n_levels           = n_levels,
    n_missing_excluded = n_missing_ex,
    model_path         = model_path_full,
    status             = "fitted",
    notes              = "",
    max_rhat           = diag$max_rhat,
    min_bulk_ess       = diag$min_bulk_ess,
    min_tail_ess       = diag$min_tail_ess,
    n_divergent        = diag$n_divergent,
    max_treedepth_hits = diag$max_treedepth_hits
  )
}

title: 21  Sensitivity analyses
text:
21.1 Overview
Sensitivity analyses repeat selected models under modified data or random-effects specifications. The primary moderators examined in sensitivity analyses are: disturbance, design, log10_years, log10_generations, trait_type, taxa.
All sensitivity models are saved in outputs/models/sensitivity/ and all summary tables in outputs/tables/sensitivity/.
Code
dat_es <- readRDS(here::here("outputs", "effect_sizes", "proceed_lnm_safe.rds"))

A_full   <- tryCatch(readRDS(here::here("outputs", "phylogeny", "proceed_A_matrix.rds")),
                     error = function(e) NULL)
name_map <- tryCatch(readRDS(here::here("outputs", "phylogeny", "proceed_name_map.rds")),
                     error = function(e) NULL)

# Apply the prepR4pcm name map so sp_ncbi_canonical is available
if (!is.null(name_map)) {
